lessons.title: Fever in Infants and Children

content_chunks.concept: Fever Without Source by Age: The Critical Algorithm
content_chunks.visual_description: Think of three risk zones: RED (danger), YELLOW (caution), GREEN (usually safe)
details: **<28 days (RED ZONE - EMERGENCY)**: ADMIT for sepsis workup! Get blood culture, urine culture, CSF culture, CXR. Start empiric IV antibiotics (ampicillin + gentamicin). Risk of serious bacterial infection ~10-15%.

**29-90 days (YELLOW ZONE - HIGH RISK)**: Temp >38°C (100.4°F) = workup needed. Full sepsis workup if ill-appearing OR fever >39°C. Well-appearing with fever <39°C: minimum UA/UCx, consider blood culture, CXR if respiratory symptoms. Close follow-up!

**>90 days (GREEN ZONE - LOWER RISK)**: If well-appearing, can often observe at home. Look for source (ear, throat, respiratory). Labs only if ill-appearing or localizing signs. Most fevers viral - don't over-test!
content_chunks.mnemonic: **<1 month = ADMIT, 1-3 months = ASSESS (labs + close f/u), >3 months = ASSESS APPEARANCE (well? go home!)**

content_chunks.visual_description: Not all thermometers are equal - route matters!
details: **Rectal**: Most accurate in infants <3 years. Use for all infants <3 months.
**Oral**: Accurate in kids ≥4 years. Can eat/drink 15 min before.
**Axillary (armpit)**: LEAST accurate - tends to read low. Don't rely on this!
**Temporal artery/tympanic**: OK for screening but not definitive in young infants
**Pacifier thermometers**: Unreliable - don't use for medical decisions
content_chunks.clinical_pearl: 📏 Rectal temp is 0.5-1°F higher than oral. Axillary is 0.5-1°F lower than oral. **Always specify route in documentation!**

content_chunks.visual_description: Picture a sick baby vs. fussy but playful baby - huge difference!
details: **ILL-APPEARING = Any of**: Lethargic/not interactive, poor eye contact, not consolable, weak cry, cyanosis, grunting, severe respiratory distress, petechiae/purpura
**WELL-APPEARING**: Alert, playful, consolable, good eye contact, normal cry, pink, feeding normally
**When in doubt, they're ill-appearing!** Over-caution is appropriate with infants.
content_chunks.clinical_pearl: 👶 **Trust parental instincts**: 'She's just not acting right' from a parent is MORE sensitive than your physical exam for serious illness!

content_chunks.visual_description: Think of fever as a symptom, not the disease - treat discomfort, not the number
details: **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)**: 10-15 mg/kg PO/PR every 4-6 hours (max 5 doses/24hr). Safe for all ages including newborns.
**Ibuprofen (Motrin/Advil)**: 10 mg/kg PO every 6-8 hours (max 40 mg/kg/day). OK for age ≥6 months only. Better for inflammatory fever.
**Alternating**: Can alternate acetaminophen and ibuprofen every 3 hours for high fevers (not routinely needed).
**DON'T USE**: Aspirin in children <18 (Reye's syndrome risk), especially with viral illness
**Cooling measures**: Lukewarm bath OK. NO ice baths, alcohol rubs (causes shivering, increases temp!)
content_chunks.clinical_pearl: 💊 Goal: Make child comfortable, NOT to normalize temperature. A happy 101°F child needs nothing!

story_intro.text: It's 2 AM. An anxious mother calls: 'My baby has a fever of 101! Should I go to the ER?' Your response depends entirely on one critical question: How old is the baby? Age determines risk. Let's master the age-based fever approach.
story_intro.visual_cue: 🌡️ Picture three babies: 3-week-old (PANIC - get to hospital!), 3-month-old (Concern - call office), 3-year-old (Calm - manage at home).

clinical_pearls: **Fever Phobia**: Educate parents that fever is protective (immune response), not dangerous per se. Brain damage doesn't occur until 107-108°F (almost impossible naturally).
**Febrile Seizures**: 2-5% of kids age 6 mo-5 yr. Simple febrile seizures (<15 min, generalized) are benign. Complex (>15 min, focal, recurrent in 24hr) need workup.
**Bundling Effect**: Overdressing can cause elevated temp in infants. If temp normalizes when undressed, not true fever.
**Teething Myth**: Teething does NOT cause high fever (>101°F) or diarrhea. If present, look for another cause.
**'Fever of Unknown Origin' (FUO)**: Fever >101°F for >14 days without identified cause despite appropriate workup. Think TB, Kawasaki, malignancy, autoimmune.
